Equilibrium concepts describe what it means for behaviour to be stable in a strategic setting. Different games require different notions of stability: simultaneous games need mutual best responses; dynamic games need credible continuation behaviour; incomplete-information games need beliefs; and communication games need consistency between messages, beliefs, and incentives.

The purpose of this page is to give a map of the main equilibrium concepts used across the notes.

## The basic question

Every equilibrium concept answers some version of the same question:

> Given what everyone else is doing, believing, or expecting, does each player have a reason to change their behaviour?

The details depend on the model. In a static game, the issue is whether anyone wants to deviate from their chosen action. In a dynamic game, we also ask whether future threats and promises are credible. In a Bayesian game, we ask whether each type of each player is acting optimally given beliefs.

## A map of equilibrium concepts

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Equilibrium Concepts] --> B[Nash Equilibrium]
    A --> C[Bayesian Nash Equilibrium]
    A --> D[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]
    A --> E[Dynamic Incomplete Information]
    A --> F[Refinements]
    A --> G[Alternative Notions]

    B --> B1[Mutual best responses]

    C --> C1[Types]
    C --> C2[Beliefs over types]

    D --> D1[Sequential rationality]
    D --> D2[Credible threats]

    E --> E1[Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium]
    E --> E2[Sequential Equilibrium]

    F --> F1[Trembling-hand Perfect]
    F --> F2[Proper Equilibrium]

    G --> G1[Correlated Equilibrium]
    G --> G2[Rationalizability]
    G --> G3[Babbling Equilibrium]
```

The map is not a strict hierarchy. Some concepts are designed for different kinds of games, while others are refinements that rule out implausible equilibria.

## Core equilibrium concepts

::: {.grid .gap-3}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}
### Nash Equilibrium

The basic equilibrium concept for strategic interaction. Each player chooses a best response to the strategies of the others.

:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}
### Subgame Perfect Equilibrium

A refinement of Nash equilibrium for dynamic games. It requires optimal behaviour after every possible history.

:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}
### Bayesian Nash Equilibrium

The basic equilibrium concept for games with incomplete information. Each type chooses optimally given beliefs about other players' types.

:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}

A dynamic incomplete-information concept combining sequential rationality with belief updating.

:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.card}
### Sequential Equilibrium

A stronger dynamic incomplete-information concept based on sequential rationality and consistent beliefs.

## Refinements and related notions

::: {.grid .gap-3}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
::: {.card}
### Trembling-hand Perfect Equilibrium

Rules out equilibria that are not robust to small mistakes.

[Open →](trembling-hand-perfect.qmd)
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
::: {.card}
### Proper Equilibrium

A stronger refinement where more costly mistakes are much less likely than less costly mistakes.

[Open →](proper-equilibrium.qmd)
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
::: {.card}
### Correlated Equilibrium

Allows players to condition actions on signals from a common recommendation device.

[Open →](correlated-equilibrium.qmd)
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
::: {.card}
### Rationalizability

Keeps strategies that can survive iterative best-response reasoning, without requiring a full equilibrium.

[Open →](rationalizability.qmd)
:::
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
::: {.card}
### Babbling Equilibrium

A cheap-talk equilibrium in which messages carry no information and are ignored by the receiver.

[Open →](babbling.qmd)
:::
:::

:::

## From basic equilibrium to refinements

A useful way to understand refinements is to ask what problem each concept tries to fix.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Nash Equilibrium] --> B[Problem: non-credible threats]
    B --> C[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]

    C --> D[Problem: beliefs after unexpected moves]
    D --> E[Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium]

    E --> F[Problem: belief consistency]
    F --> G[Sequential Equilibrium]

    A --> H[Problem: fragile equilibria]
    H --> I[Trembling-hand Perfect Equilibrium]
    I --> J[Proper Equilibrium]
```

Nash equilibrium is the starting point. Refinements add extra discipline when the basic idea of mutual best response is not enough.

## Choosing the right concept

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[What kind of game is it?] --> B[Simultaneous and complete information]
    A --> C[Sequential and complete information]
    A --> D[Static incomplete information]
    A --> E[Dynamic incomplete information]
    A --> F[Cheap talk or communication]
    A --> G[Recommendation device or mediated play]

    B --> B1[Nash Equilibrium]
    C --> C1[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]
    D --> D1[Bayesian Nash Equilibrium]
    E --> E1[Perfect Bayesian or Sequential Equilibrium]
    F --> F1[Informative or Babbling Equilibrium]
    G --> G1[Correlated Equilibrium]
```

This decision tree is only a guide. In actual modelling, the right solution concept depends on what the model needs to explain.

## Comparison table

| Concept | Used for | Core requirement | Main issue addressed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nash equilibrium | Static games | Mutual best responses | Strategic stability |
| Subgame perfect equilibrium | Dynamic complete-information games | Nash equilibrium in every subgame | Credibility |
| Bayesian Nash equilibrium | Static incomplete-information games | Type-contingent best responses | Private information |
| Perfect Bayesian equilibrium | Dynamic incomplete-information games | Sequential rationality and beliefs | Off-path inference |
| Sequential equilibrium | Dynamic incomplete-information games | Sequential rationality and consistent beliefs | Stronger belief discipline |
| Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium | Strategic-form games | Robustness to small mistakes | Fragile equilibria |
| Proper equilibrium | Strategic-form games | Costlier mistakes are less likely | Stronger mistake discipline |
| Correlated equilibrium | Games with recommendations | Obedience to signals | Coordination through information |
| Rationalizability | Strategic reasoning | Survival under best-response reasoning | Reasoning without full equilibrium |
| Babbling equilibrium | Cheap-talk games | Messages ignored by receiver | No information transmission |

## Why equilibrium is not enough

An equilibrium can be stable but undesirable. It can also be mathematically valid but behaviourally implausible. This is why equilibrium analysis usually needs interpretation.

When reading an equilibrium result, ask:

1. What incentives make this behaviour stable?
2. What beliefs support the behaviour?
3. Are threats and promises credible?
4. Is the equilibrium efficient or inefficient?
5. Are there multiple equilibria?
6. Would the result survive small changes in assumptions?

These questions matter because equilibrium is a tool for explanation, not a guarantee of realism.
